# Gandhabbakāya Saṁyutta (SN 31)
**ID:** SN 31
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Gandhabbakāya Saṁyutta* (SN 31), translated as the "Linked Discourses on Centaurs", is the thirty-first division of the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003; SuttaCentral]. It constitutes the third of a group of four contiguous collections focused on the conditions and modes under which beings achieve rebirth among various semi-celestial orders [SuttaCentral; Rhys Davids 1924]. In Buddhist lore, *gandhabbas* are minor deities—often compared to centaurs or fairies—traditionally associated with music, conception, and aromatic vegetation [SuttaCentral; Rhys Davids 1924; Bodhi 2003]. Throughout the collection, the Buddha explains to questioning monks the causes leading to rebirth in the company of these *gandhabbakāyikā devā* [Rhys Davids 1924; Hazra 1994]. In particular, these beings are described as inhabiting various fragrant botanical parts, including roots, heartwood, pith, bark, sap, leaves, flowers, and scents [Hazra 1994; Bodhi 2003]. According to the commentary, the name is linked to the stem *gandha* ("scent"), and rebirth into specific sub-classes of these beings corresponds systematically to individual gifts of fragrant materials offered by the practitioner [Bodhi 2003].
Curated cross-tradition parallels on SuttaCentral identify corresponding discourses in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* at SĀ 128–129 [SuttaCentral], although twentieth-century comparative surveys noted the samyutta's absence or substantial abbreviation in early comparative tables of the Chinese Āgamas [Dutt 1978]. Computational text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus demonstrates heavy structural parallels across 42 other Pali texts (1,423 matches), reflecting recurrent formulaic exposition shared with the companion collections *Nāga Saṁyutta* (SN 29), *Valāhaka Saṁyutta* (SN 32), and *Supaṇṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 30), as well as the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta* (MN 120) and the *Aṭṭhakanipāta* (AN 8) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments detected by DharmaNexus connect these passages to the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma *Dharmaskandha*, the Chinese *Qishi yinben jing* (起世因本經, T 25) and *Madhyama Āgama* (中阿含經, T 26), and related Tibetan canonical and scholastic excerpts [DharmaNexus].
